cor-mat-generalized-rayleigh.title: Relative to a positive definite matrix
cor-mat-generalized-rayleigh.title_html: Relative to a positive definite matrix
cor-mat-generalized-rayleigh.html:
Let A be symmetric and B positive definite, both n×n.

  1. maxx≠0x⊤Ax/x⊤Bx is the largest eigenvalue of B−1A, which has the same eigenvalues as the symmetric B−1/2AB−1/2.

  2. There is a nonsingular P with P⊤BP=I and P⊤AP diagonal.

  3. For a∈Rn, maxx≠0(a⊤x)2/x⊤Bx=a⊤B−1a, attained at x=B−1a.

cor-mat-invariant.title: Invariant linear functions
cor-mat-invariant.html: Let Ax=b be consistent and let q∈Rn. The value q⊤x is the same for every solution x iff q∈C(A⊤), that is, iff q⊤=q⊤GA for one (and then every) generalized inverse G.

cor-mat-spectral-consequences.html:
Let A=QΛQ⊤ be symmetric.

  1. rank(A) counts the nonzero eigenvalues. C(A) is spanned by the qi with λi≠0, and N(A) by those with λi=0.

  2. Ak=QΛkQ⊤ for k=1,2,…. If A is nonsingular, A−1=QΛ−1Q⊤, and A+=QΛ+Q⊤ in general, where Λ+ inverts the nonzero diagonal entries.

  3. The eigenspace {x:Ax=λx} has dimension equal to the multiplicity of λ as a root of the characteristic polynomial.

def-mat-condition-number.title: Condition number
def-mat-condition-number.html: The condition number of an m×n matrix A of full column rank is κ(A)=σmax(A)σmin(A)=σ1σn. For a nonsingular square matrix this equals ‖A‖2‖A−1‖2. A matrix without full column rank has κ(A)=∞ by convention.

def-mat-ginverse.title: Generalized inverse
def-mat-ginverse.html: A generalized inverse of an m×n matrix A is any n×m matrix A− with AA−A=A.

def-mat-kronecker.html: The Kronecker product of an m×n matrix A and a p×q matrix B is the mp×nq block matrix A⊗B=(aijB). The vec operator places the n columns of an m×n matrix one below another, giving a vector of length mn: vec(A)=(a1⊤,…,an⊤)⊤.

def-mat-moore-penrose.title: Moore–Penrose inverse
def-mat-moore-penrose.html: The Moore–Penrose inverse of A is the matrix A+ satisfying AA+A=A,A+AA+=A+,(AA+)⊤=AA+,(A+A)⊤=A+A.

def-mat-nnd.html: A symmetric matrix A is positive definite if x⊤Ax>0 for every x≠0, and nonnegative definite if x⊤Ax≥0 for every x. For symmetric A,B of the same size we write A⪰B if A−B is nonnegative definite, and A≻B if it is positive definite (the Loewner order).

def-mat-schur.title: Schur complement
def-mat-schur.html: If A11 is nonsingular, the Schur complement of A11 in A is A22⋅1=A22−A21A11−1A12. If A22 is nonsingular, the Schur complement of A22 is A11⋅2=A11−A12A22−1A21.

eq-mat-block-ldu.html: A=(I0A21A11−1I)(A1100A22⋅1)(IA11−1A120I).

eq-mat-frobenius.html: ∑i,jaij2=∑j‖aj‖2,

eq-mat-general-solution.html: {Gb+(I−GA)z:z∈Rn}=x0+N(A).

eq-mat-kappa-squared.html: κ(A⊤A)=κ(A)2.

eq-mat-leading-block.html: (A11−A12A22−1A21)−1=A11−1+A11−1A12A22⋅1−1A21A11−1.

eq-mat-partition.html: A=(A11A12A21A22),

eq-mat-partitioned-inverse.html: A−1=(A11−1+A11−1A12A22⋅1−1A21A11−1−A11−1A12A22⋅1−1−A22⋅1−1A21A11−1A22⋅1−1).

eq-mat-perturbation.html: ‖δx‖‖x‖≤‖A−1‖2‖δb‖‖b‖/σ1=κ(A)‖δb‖‖b‖.

eq-mat-product-readings.html: Ab=∑j=1nbjaj,AB=[Ab1,…,Abq],AB=∑k=1nakb(k)⊤.

eq-mat-rayleigh.html: λn≤x⊤Axx⊤x≤λ1,

eq-mat-sherman-morrison.html: (B+uv⊤)−1=B−1−B−1uv⊤B−11+v⊤B−1u.

eq-mat-skeleton.html: A=A⋅JAIJ−1AI⋅,

eq-mat-spectral.html: A=QΛQ⊤=∑i=1nλiqiqi⊤,Λ=diag(λ1,…,λn).

eq-mat-svd.html: A=UDV⊤=∑i=1rσiuivi⊤,D=diag(σ1,…,σr).

eq-mat-symmetrize.html: x⊤Ax=x⊤(12(A+A⊤))x.

eq-mat-trace-tricks.html: tr(A⊤A)=∑i,jaij2=‖A‖F2,x⊤Ax=tr(Axx⊤),tr(P−1AP)=tr(A).

eq-mat-transpose-product.html: (AB)⊤=B⊤A⊤.

eq-mat-woodbury.html: (B+UCV⊤)−1=B−1−B−1U(C−1+V⊤B−1U)−1V⊤B−1.

exm-mat-centring.title: Sums of squares as quadratic forms
exm-mat-centring.title_html: Sums of squares as quadratic forms
exm-mat-centring.html: The sum of squared deviations of y∈Rn from its mean is ∑i=1n(yi−y¯)2=y⊤y−ny¯2=y⊤(In−1nJn)y, because ny¯2=(1⊤y)2/n=y⊤Jny/n. The centring matrix In−n−1Jn is symmetric and satisfies (In−n−1Jn)2=In−n−1Jn, because Jn2=nJn. Every sum of squares in an analysis of variance is a quadratic form whose matrix has these two properties (Section 1.9).

exm-mat-deletion.title: Deleting an observation
exm-mat-deletion.html: Removing the ith row xi⊤ from a model matrix changes X⊤X into X⊤X−xixi⊤. With u=−xi, v=xi and hi=xi⊤(X⊤X)−1xi, @eq-mat-sherman-morrison gives (X⊤X−xixi⊤)−1=(X⊤X)−1+(X⊤X)−1xixi⊤(X⊤X)−11−hi, valid whenever hi<1, and the determinant lemma gives det(X⊤X−xixi⊤)=(1−hi)det(X⊤X). The quantity hi is the leverage of observation i (Chapter 6), and these formulas are what make the deletion diagnostics of Chapter 20 cheap. For Brownlee’s stack-loss data (n=21, p=4), the listing updates the inverse for each of the 21 deletions. The largest relative discrepancy from direct inversion is 1×10−13. Observation 17 has the largest leverage, 0.412, and removing it multiplies det(X⊤X) by 0.588.

exm-mat-equicorrelation.title: Equicorrelation
exm-mat-equicorrelation.html: The matrix E=(1−ρ)In+ρJn has unit diagonal and every off-diagonal entry equal to ρ. It is the correlation matrix of exchangeable observations. Taking B=(1−ρ)I and u=ρ1, v=1, for ρ≠1 and 1+(n−1)ρ≠0, E−1=11−ρ(In−ρ1+(n−1)ρJn),detE=(1−ρ)n−1(1+(n−1)ρ).

exm-mat-equicorrelation-eigen.title: Eigenvalues of the equicorrelation matrix
exm-mat-equicorrelation-eigen.html: For E=(1−ρ)I+ρJn of @exm-mat-equicorrelation, E1=(1+(n−1)ρ)1, and Ev=(1−ρ)v for every v⊥1. So the eigenvalues are 1+(n−1)ρ once and 1−ρ with multiplicity n−1, with eigenvectors 1/n and the last n−1 rows of the Helmert matrix (@exm-mat-helmert). The determinant and inverse found earlier follow at once from @prp-mat-eigen-basic and @cor-mat-spectral-consequences(b).

exm-mat-factor.title: Diagonal plus low rank
exm-mat-factor.html: In factor models and in the linear mixed models of Chapter 32, covariance matrices have the form Σ=D+LL⊤ with D diagonal and positive and L of size N×k, k≪N. By @eq-mat-woodbury and @thm-mat-block-determinant(c), Σ−1=D−1−D−1L(Ik+L⊤D−1L)−1L⊤D−1,detΣ=detDdet(Ik+L⊤D−1L). Each needs only a k×k factorization. The script checks this with N=1500 and k=4. The solution of Σw=v agrees with a direct solve to a relative error of 8×10−14.

exm-mat-helmert.title: Helmert matrices
exm-mat-helmert.html: The n×n Helmert matrix H has first row n−1/21⊤ and, for k=2,…,n, kth row hk⊤=1k(k−1)(1,…,1⏟k−1,−(k−1),0,…,0). Each row has unit length, since (k−1)+(k−1)2=k(k−1). Row k is orthogonal to row 1 because its entries sum to zero. For 2≤j<k, the nonzero entries of hj sit in positions 1,…,j, where hk is constant, so hj⊤hk is proportional to the sum of the entries of hj, which is zero. So H is orthogonal. For y∈Rn, (Hy)1=ny¯ and, by @prp-mat-orthogonal(a), ∑k=2n(hk⊤y)2=‖Hy‖2−ny¯2=∑i=1n(yi−y¯)2. The sum of squared deviations is a sum of n−1 squares of orthonormal contrasts. With independent normal observations this gives a short proof that the sample mean and variance are independent (@exr-mvn-rotation).

exm-mat-ls-gradient.title: The least squares criterion
exm-mat-ls-gradient.html: Let S(b)=‖y−Xb‖2=y⊤y−2y⊤Xb+b⊤X⊤Xb. By @thm-mat-quadform-derivative, ∂S∂b=−2X⊤y+2X⊤Xb=−2X⊤(y−Xb),∂2S∂b∂b⊤=2X⊤X. Setting the gradient to zero gives the normal equations X⊤Xb=X⊤y. The Hessian is nonnegative definite, so S is convex and every solution is a global minimizer. The next result proves this without calculus, and covers the rank-deficient case.

exm-mat-macro-svd.title: A macroeconomic design
exm-mat-macro-svd.html:
Take the 203 quarterly US observations of real GDP, real investment, real government spending, real disposable income, population and unemployment, with an intercept, as a model matrix with p=7 columns. As recorded, κ(X)=5.10×105. Most of that is units: GDP is measured in billions and unemployment in percent. Rescaling each column to unit length reduces it to 383, and centring the regressors before rescaling reduces it further to 124. By @eq-mat-kappa-squared the corresponding cross-product matrix has condition number 15386.

What remains is not an artefact of units. Figure 1.8.1(b) shows the right singular vector for the smallest singular value, σmin=0.0175, of the centred and scaled design. Its weight is concentrated on GDP (0.78) and disposable income (−0.61). The combination of the scaled columns with these coefficients is a vector of length 0.0175, although every column has length one. The two series move almost in lockstep: their correlation is 0.9990. No rescaling can separate their coefficients well. Centring is not a neutral choice, however: it removes near-dependences that involve the intercept, and Belsley et al. (1980) recommend scaling without centring for that reason, so their diagnostics would use the unit-length figure 383. Chapter 26 returns to the choice. The listing computes the singular values, and the script also checks @eq-mat-kappa-squared, the Penrose conditions for VD−1U⊤, and the Eckart–Young bound.

exm-mat-margins.title: Filling a table from its margins
exm-mat-margins.title_html: Filling a table from its margins
exm-mat-margins.html:
Suppose the six entries of a 2×3 table are unknown, but its row totals (9,6) and column totals (4,5,6) are known. With the cells ordered x11,x12,x13,x21,x22,x23, the equations are Ax=b with A=(111000000111100100010010001001),b=(96456). The rows of A satisfy one relation: the two row-total rows and the three column-total rows both add to 16⊤. So rank(A)=4 and there is a 6−4=2-dimensional family of solutions. The same relation must hold for b. By @thm-mat-consistency(c), the system is consistent iff the row totals and the column totals have the same sum, and here both sums are 15.

The listing builds three generalized inverses: G1 from the nonsingular submatrix in rows 1–4 and columns 1–4 (@thm-mat-ginverse-exists), the Moore–Penrose inverse G2=A+, and G3=G1+(I−G1A)Z for an integer matrix Z (@prp-mat-ginverse-props(e)). They give the solutions \[ \begin{aligned} \G_1\bb&=(-2,\ 5,\ 6,\ 6,\ 0,\ 0)\T, & \norm{\G_1\bb}&=10.050,\ \G_2\bb&=(5/2,\ 3,\ 7/2,\ 3/2,\ 2,\ 5/2)\T, & \norm{\G_2\bb}&=6.325,\ \G_3\bb&=(21,\ -}39,\ 27,\ \ensuremath{-}17,\ 44,\ \ensuremath{-21)\T, & \norm{\G_3\bb}&=73.192.\end{aligned} \] The individual cell x11 takes the values −2, 5/2 and 21: margins do not determine cells. But x12+x13−x21 equals 5 for all three, as @cor-mat-invariant predicts, because its coefficient vector is the first row of A minus the third. The minimum-norm solution has the additive form xij=ri/3+cj/2−15/6 in terms of the row totals ri and column totals cj (@exr-mat-margins-min-norm). If the last column total is changed to 7, then AGb≠b for each of the three matrices, and the script confirms that the test detects the inconsistency. The script also checks all 60 submatrices formed by 4 independent rows and 4 independent columns, and finds each one nonsingular, as @prp-mat-nonsingular-submatrix requires.

exm-mat-two-way-kronecker.title: The balanced two-way layout
exm-mat-two-way-kronecker.html: Let observations yij, i=1,…,a, j=1,…,b, be stacked with j running inside i. The additive model E(yij)=μ+αi+βj has model matrix X=[1a⊗1b, Ia⊗1b, 1a⊗Ib], because Ia⊗1b has a 1 in column i exactly for the b observations in row i. With J¯k=k−1Jk, a symmetric idempotent averaging matrix, the mixed-product rule shows that Ia⊗J¯b, J¯a⊗Ib and J¯a⊗J¯b replace each observation by its row mean, its column mean and the grand mean. The matrix M=Ia⊗J¯b+J¯a⊗Ib−J¯a⊗J¯b is symmetric and idempotent, with trace a+b−1=rank(X). It is the projection onto C(X) (Chapter 15). The script checks this for a=3 and b=4, together with each part of @prp-mat-kronecker.

exr-mat-2x2-definite.title: A1
exr-mat-2x2-definite.html: Show that (abbc) is positive definite iff a>0 and ac>b2, and nonnegative definite iff a≥0, c≥0 and ac≥b2. Why is a≥0 and ac≥b2 not enough?

exr-mat-adding-regressors.title: B2
exr-mat-adding-regressors.html: Let X=[X1,X2] have full column rank. Show that the leading block of (X⊤X)−1 satisfies [(X⊤X)−1]11⪰(X1⊤X1)−1, with equality iff X1⊤X2=0. Interpret this for the variances of least squares coefficients when regressors are added to a model.

exr-mat-bordered.title: A2
exr-mat-bordered.html: Let A be nonsingular, a a vector and c a scalar with s=c−a⊤A−1a≠0. Write down the inverse and the determinant of (Aaa⊤c). Use it to update (X⊤X)−1 when a column is added to X.

exr-mat-cancellation.title: A2
exr-mat-cancellation.html: Show that X⊤XB=X⊤XC implies XB=XC. Deduce that X⊤Xb=0 iff Xb=0.

exr-mat-clustered.title: A1
exr-mat-clustered.html: Observations fall in a clusters of size b, and Σ=σ2Ia⊗Eb, where Eb=(1−ρ)Ib+ρJb. Find the eigenvalues, determinant and inverse of Σ using @prp-mat-kronecker, @exm-mat-equicorrelation and @exm-mat-equicorrelation-eigen.

exr-mat-cond-scaling.title: B2
exr-mat-cond-scaling.html: Show that κ(X)≥maxj‖xj‖/mink‖xk‖, so that columns on very different scales force a large condition number. Show by example that rescaling the columns can also increase κ.

exr-mat-cond-two.title: B1
exr-mat-cond-two.html: Let X=[x1,x2] with ‖x1‖=‖x2‖=1 and x1⊤x2=r, |r|<1. Show that κ(X)=(1+|r|)/(1−|r|). How large must |r| be for κ(X)>30?

exr-mat-consistency-numeric.title: A3
exr-mat-consistency-numeric.html: For which c and d is the system x1+x2+x3=2, x1−x2=c, 3x1+x2+2x3=d consistent? When it is, give its general solution in the form @eq-mat-general-solution.

exr-mat-constrained-ls.title: B1
exr-mat-constrained-ls.html: Let X have full column rank, β^=(X⊤X)−1X⊤y, and let H be q×p with full row rank. Show that the minimizer of ‖y−Xb‖2 subject to Hb=h is β^H=β^−(X⊤X)−1H⊤W−1(Hβ^−h),W=H(X⊤X)−1H⊤, and that the increase in the residual sum of squares is (Hβ^−h)⊤W−1(Hβ^−h).

exr-mat-courant-fischer.title: C1
exr-mat-courant-fischer.html: Let A be symmetric with eigenvalues λ1≥⋯≥λn. Prove the Courant–Fischer theorem λk=maxdim⁡S=k min0≠x∈Sx⊤Axx⊤x. Deduce that if B is obtained from A by deleting one row and the corresponding column, its eigenvalues μ1≥⋯≥μn−1 interlace: λk≥μk≥λk+1.

exr-mat-householder.title: B1
exr-mat-householder.html: Let u be a unit vector and H=I−2uu⊤. Show that H is symmetric and orthogonal, that Hu=−u, and that Hv=v for v⊥u. Given x not a nonnegative multiple of e1, find u with Hx=‖x‖e1. Explain how repeating this column by column produces a QR factorization.

exr-mat-idempotent-products.title: A1
exr-mat-idempotent-products.html: Let A,B be idempotent of the same size. Show that AB is idempotent if AB=BA, and that A+B is idempotent iff AB+BA=0. Show that the latter forces AB=0 (symmetry is not needed).

exr-mat-independent-solutions.title: B3
exr-mat-independent-solutions.html: Let A be m×n of rank r and let Ax=b be consistent with b≠0. Show that the system has n−r+1 linearly independent solutions and no more, and that every solution is an affine combination of them.

exr-mat-leave-one-out.title: B1
exr-mat-leave-one-out.html: Let β^=(X⊤X)−1X⊤y, ei=yi−xi⊤β^ and hi=xi⊤(X⊤X)−1xi<1. Show that the least squares coefficients computed without observation i are β^(i)=β^−(X⊤X)−1xiei1−hi.

exr-mat-loewner-det.title: B1
exr-mat-loewner-det.html: Let A⪰B≻0. Show that detA≥detB and trA≥trB.

exr-mat-margins-min-norm.title: A2
exr-mat-margins-min-norm.html: Generalize @exm-mat-margins to an a×b table with row totals ri, column totals cj and grand total T=∑iri=∑jcj. Show that xij=ri/b+cj/a−T/(ab) is a solution lying in C(A⊤), and hence is the minimum-norm solution.

exr-mat-mp-factorization.title: B2
exr-mat-mp-factorization.html: Let A=BF be a rank factorization. Show that A+=F⊤(FF⊤)−1(B⊤B)−1B⊤. Deduce that A+=(A⊤A)−1A⊤ when A has full column rank.

exr-mat-mp-properties.title: C1
exr-mat-mp-properties.html: Show that (A+)+=A, (A⊤)+=(A+)⊤, (A⊤A)+=A+(A+)⊤ and A+=(A⊤A)+A⊤. Give an example with (AB)+≠B+A+.

exr-mat-normal-mle.title: C2
exr-mat-normal-mle.html: Let S be positive definite of size p×p. Show that g(Σ)=−log⁡detΣ−tr(Σ−1S), over positive definite Σ, is maximized uniquely at Σ=S. Hint: write g in terms of the eigenvalues of S−1/2ΣS−1/2.

exr-mat-oblique.title: B1
exr-mat-oblique.html: Let A be idempotent. Show that A is symmetric iff C(A)⊥N(A).

exr-mat-pairwise.title: A1
exr-mat-pairwise.html: Show that ∑i<j(yi−yj)2=n∑i(yi−y¯)2, and write both sides as y⊤Ay with A symmetric. Find the symmetric matrix of the quadratic form 2x12−x22+6x1x2−4x2x3.

exr-mat-push-through.title: B2
exr-mat-push-through.html: For an n×p matrix X and λ>0, show that (X⊤X+λIp)−1X⊤=X⊤(XX⊤+λIn)−1. Explain why the right-hand side is preferable when p is much larger than n, and derive the identity a second way from @thm-mat-woodbury.

exr-mat-qr-unique.title: B2
exr-mat-qr-unique.html: Show that the QR factorization of a matrix with full column rank, with R having positive diagonal, is unique, and that R⊤ is the Cholesky factor of X⊤X.

exr-mat-rank-factorization.title: B2
exr-mat-rank-factorization.html: Show that if A=B1F1=B2F2 are two rank factorizations, then B2=B1T and F2=T−1F1 for a nonsingular T.

exr-mat-reflexive.title: B1
exr-mat-reflexive.html: Let G be a generalized inverse of A. Show that GAG=G iff rank(G)=rank(A).

exr-mat-ridge.title: A2
exr-mat-ridge.html: Use @prp-mat-quadratic-min to show that ‖y−Xb‖2+λ‖b‖2 with λ>0 has the unique minimizer (X⊤X+λI)−1X⊤y, whatever the rank of X.

exr-mat-rotations.title: A1
exr-mat-rotations.html: Show that every 2×2 orthogonal matrix is either a rotation (cos⁡θ−sin⁡θsin⁡θcos⁡θ) (determinant 1) or a reflection (cos⁡θsin⁡θsin⁡θ−cos⁡θ) (determinant −1). Find the line fixed by the reflection.

exr-mat-sylvester.title: B1
exr-mat-sylvester.html: Let A be m×n and B be n×q. Prove rank(AB)≥rank(A)+rank(B)−n. Hint: apply rank–nullity to AB0, where the columns of B0 are a basis of C(B).

exr-mat-trace-order.title: A1
exr-mat-trace-order.html: Show that tr(ABC)=tr(ACB) when A,B,C are symmetric, and find 2×2 matrices for which the two traces differ.

exr-mat-two-way-rank.title: A3
exr-mat-two-way-rank.html: For the additive two-way layout with two rows, three columns and one observation per cell, write the 6×6 model matrix X=[1,R,C], where R and C hold the row and column indicators. Find rank(X) and a basis of N(X). Compare [R,C]⊤ with the matrix A of @exm-mat-margins.

exr-mat-vector-ginverse.title: A1
exr-mat-vector-ginverse.html: Find all generalized inverses of a nonzero vector a∈Rn, regarded as an n×1 matrix. Which one is a+?

prp-mat-cauchy-schwarz.title: Cauchy–Schwarz
prp-mat-cauchy-schwarz.html: For u,v∈Rn, (u⊤v)2≤(u⊤u)(v⊤v), with equality iff one vector is a multiple of the other. Consequently ‖u+v‖≤‖u‖+‖v‖.

prp-mat-complement.html:
Let A be m×n and let S⊆Rn be a subspace.

  1. N(A)=C(A⊤)⊥ and N(A⊤)=C(A)⊥.

  2. dim⁡S⊥=n−dim⁡S, and Rn=S⊕S⊥. In particular Rn=C(A⊤)⊕N(A) and Rm=C(A)⊕N(A⊤).

  3. (S⊥)⊥=S.

prp-mat-det.title: Determinants
prp-mat-det.html:
Let A,B be n×n.

  1. detA⊤=detA.

  2. detA is a linear function of each column separately. It changes sign when two columns are interchanged, and is unchanged when a multiple of one column is added to another. The same holds for rows.

  3. A triangular matrix has determinant equal to the product of its diagonal entries.

  4. det(AB)=detAdetB.

  5. A is nonsingular iff detA≠0, and then detA−1=1/detA.

  6. det(cA)=cndetA, and detQ=±1 for orthogonal Q.

prp-mat-eigen-basic.html:
Let A be n×n with eigenvalues λ1,…,λn.

  1. detA=∏iλi and trA=∑iλi.

  2. If Ax=λx, then f(A)x=f(λ)x for every polynomial f. If A is nonsingular, A−1x=λ−1x.

  3. A and P−1AP have the same characteristic polynomial for nonsingular P.

  4. If C is m×n and D is n×m, then λndet(λIm−CD)=λmdet(λIn−DC). So CD and DC have the same nonzero eigenvalues, with the same multiplicities.

prp-mat-ginverse-props.title: Properties of generalized inverses
prp-mat-ginverse-props.html:
Let A be m×n of rank r and let G be a generalized inverse of A.

  1. AG and GA are idempotent. Moreover C(AG)=C(A) and N(GA)=N(A), and rank(AG)=rank(GA)=r≤rank(G).

  2. G⊤ is a generalized inverse of A⊤.

  3. If G1,G2 are generalized inverses of A, so is G1AG2. In particular GAG is a generalized inverse which also satisfies (GAG)A(GAG)=GAG.

  4. If A is symmetric, then G⊤ and 12(G+G⊤) are generalized inverses of A, so a symmetric generalized inverse always exists.

  5. G+(I−GA)U+V(I−AG) is a generalized inverse of A for every U and V of size n×m.

prp-mat-idempotent-basic.title: General idempotent matrices
prp-mat-idempotent-basic.html:
Let A be n×n and idempotent of rank r.

  1. Every eigenvalue of A is 0 or 1.

  2. rank(A)=tr(A).

  3. I−A is idempotent, A(I−A)=(I−A)A=0, C(I−A)=N(A), and rank(A)+rank(I−A)=n.

  4. An idempotent matrix that is nonsingular equals I.

  5. P−1AP is idempotent for nonsingular P, and A⊤ is idempotent.

prp-mat-inverse.html: For an n×n matrix A the following are equivalent: (a) A is nonsingular; (b) rank(A)=n; (c) N(A)={0}; (d) BA=I for some B; (e) AC=I for some C. When they hold, B=C=A−1, and (A⊤)−1=(A−1)⊤,(AB)−1=B−1A−1 for nonsingular A,B of the same size. A nonsingular symmetric matrix has a symmetric inverse.

prp-mat-kronecker.html:
For matrices of compatible sizes:

  1. (A⊗B)(C⊗D)=AC⊗BD (mixed-product rule);

  2. (A⊗B)⊤=A⊤⊗B⊤, and (A⊗B)−1=A−1⊗B−1 for nonsingular A,B. More generally A−⊗B− is a generalized inverse of A⊗B;

  3. tr(A⊗B)=tr(A)tr(B) and rank(A⊗B)=rank(A)rank(B);

  4. if A (m×m) and B (p×p) are symmetric with eigenvalues λi and μj, the eigenvalues of A⊗B are the products λiμj, and det(A⊗B)=(detA)p(detB)m;

  5. Kronecker products of orthogonal, symmetric, idempotent, or nonnegative definite matrices are of the same kind;

  6. vec(ABC)=(C⊤⊗A)vec(B) and tr(A⊤B)=vec(A)⊤vec(B).

prp-mat-lagrange.html: Let A be positive definite, H of size q×n with full row rank, and f(x)=x⊤Ax−2b⊤x. The unique minimizer of f subject to Hx=h is x∗=x0−A−1H⊤(HA−1H⊤)−1(Hx0−h),x0=A−1b.

prp-mat-matrix-derivatives.html:
1. ∂tr(AW)/∂W=A⊤.

  2. If detW>0, then ∂log⁡detW/∂W=(W−1)⊤.

  3. If A(t) is a nonsingular matrix whose entries are differentiable functions of a scalar t, with derivative A˙=∂A/∂t, then ∂A−1∂t=−A−1A˙A−1,∂log⁡|detA|∂t=tr(A−1A˙).

prp-mat-min-norm.title: Minimum-norm solution
prp-mat-min-norm.html: If Ax=b is consistent, then A+b is its unique solution lying in C(A⊤), and ‖A+b‖<‖x‖ for every other solution x.

prp-mat-nonsingular-submatrix.html:
Let A have rank r≥1. Choose any r linearly independent rows, indexed by I, and any r linearly independent columns, indexed by J. Then the r×r submatrix AIJ at their intersection is nonsingular, and A=A⋅JAIJ−1AI⋅,{#eq-mat-skeleton}

where A⋅J holds the columns in J and AI⋅ the rows in I.

prp-mat-orthogonal.html:
Let Q and P be n×n orthogonal matrices.

  1. (Qx)⊤(Qv)=x⊤v and ‖Qx‖=‖x‖ for all x,v.

  2. Q⊤ and QP are orthogonal.

  3. Every entry satisfies |qij|≤1, and detQ=±1.

  4. If [Q1,Q2] is orthogonal with Q1 of size n×r, then Q1Q1⊤+Q2Q2⊤=In, and C(Q2)=C(Q1)⊥.

prp-mat-pd-properties.html:
Let A be n×n nonnegative definite.

  1. aii≥0, and if aii=0 then row i and column i of A are zero.

  2. x⊤Ax=0 iff Ax=0.

  3. B⊤AB is nonnegative definite for any n×q matrix B. If A is positive definite, B⊤AB is positive definite iff B has full column rank.

  4. Every principal submatrix of A is nonnegative definite, and positive definite if A is.

  5. If A is positive definite, it is nonsingular and A−1 is positive definite. If also A is partitioned as in @eq-mat-partition, both Schur complements A11⋅2 and A22⋅1 are positive definite.

  6. If A⪰B≻0, then B−1⪰A−1.

prp-mat-quadratic-min.title: Minimizing a quadratic function
prp-mat-quadratic-min.html: Let A be n×n nonnegative definite, b∈Rn and f(x)=x⊤Ax−2b⊤x. If b∈C(A), the minimizers of f are exactly the solutions of Ax=b, and the minimum value is −b⊤A−b for any generalized inverse A−. If b∉C(A), then f is unbounded below.

prp-mat-rank-product.html:
Let A be m×n and B be n×q.

  1. C(AB)⊆C(A) and N(B)⊆N(AB), so rank(AB)≤min{rank(A),rank(B)}.

  2. If B has full row rank, then C(AB)=C(A). If A has full column rank, then N(AB)=N(B). So rank(AB)=rank(A) in the first case and rank(AB)=rank(B) in the second. In particular, multiplying by a nonsingular matrix does not change rank.

  3. N(A⊤A)=N(A) and C(A⊤A)=C(A⊤), so rank(A⊤A)=rank(AA⊤)=rank(A).

  4. rank(A+C)≤rank(A)+rank(C) for C of the same size as A.

prp-mat-svd-norms.title: Norms and extremal properties
prp-mat-svd-norms.html:
Let A be m×n with singular values σ1≥σ2≥⋯, and let ‖A‖2=maxx≠0‖Ax‖/‖x‖ be the spectral norm.

  1. ‖A‖2=σ1 and ‖A‖F2=∑iσi2.

  2. If A has full column rank n, then minx≠0‖Ax‖/‖x‖=σn, attained at vn.

  3. (Eckart–Young.) For k<r, let Ak=∑i≤kσiuivi⊤. Then ‖A−B‖2≥σk+1=‖A−Ak‖2 for every B with rank(B)≤k.

thm-mat-block-determinant.title: Block determinants
thm-mat-block-determinant.html:
Let A be partitioned as in @eq-mat-partition.

  1. If A12=0 or A21=0, then detA=detA11detA22.

  2. If A11 is nonsingular, detA=detA11detA22⋅1. If A22 is nonsingular, detA=detA22detA11⋅2.

  3. For m×n matrices U and n×m matrices V, det(Im+UV)=det(In+VU). If B is m×m and nonsingular, det(B+UV)=detBdet(In+VB−1U).

thm-mat-consistency.title: Consistency and the general solution
thm-mat-consistency.html:
Let G be any generalized inverse of A. The following are equivalent:

  1. Ax=b is consistent;

  2. b∈C(A);

  3. rank[A,b]=rank(A);

  4. AGb=b.

If the system is consistent, x0=Gb is a solution, and the set of all solutions is {Gb+(I−GA)z:z∈Rn}=x0+N(A).{#eq-mat-general-solution}

thm-mat-extremal-rayleigh.title: Rayleigh quotient
thm-mat-extremal-rayleigh.html:
Let A be symmetric with eigenvalues λ1≥⋯≥λn and orthonormal eigenvectors q1,…,qn. For every x≠0, λn≤x⊤Axx⊤x≤λ1,{#eq-mat-rayleigh}

with equality on the right at x=q1 and on the left at x=qn. More generally, the maximum of x⊤Ax/x⊤x over nonzero x orthogonal to q1,…,qk−1 is λk, attained at qk.

thm-mat-ginverse-exists.title: Existence
thm-mat-ginverse-exists.html: Every matrix has a generalized inverse. Explicitly, if rank(A)=r≥1 and AIJ is the nonsingular r×r submatrix of @prp-mat-nonsingular-submatrix, the n×m matrix G that holds AIJ−1 in the rows indexed by J and the columns indexed by I, and zeros elsewhere, is a generalized inverse of A.

thm-mat-idempotent.title: Symmetric idempotent matrices
thm-mat-idempotent.html:
Let A be an n×n symmetric matrix of rank r. Then A is idempotent iff all its eigenvalues are 0 or 1. In that case

  1. A=Q1Q1⊤, where the n×r matrix Q1 has orthonormal columns spanning C(A);

  2. rank(A)=tr(A)=r, the multiplicity of the eigenvalue 1;

  3. A and I−A are nonnegative definite, and x⊤Ax=‖Ax‖2≤‖x‖2.

thm-mat-idempotent-sum.title: Sums of symmetric idempotent matrices
thm-mat-idempotent-sum.html:
Let A1,…,Ak be symmetric n×n matrices and A=∑iAi. Consider

  1. A is idempotent;

  2. every Ai is idempotent;

  3. AiAj=0 for all i≠j.

Any two of these imply the third. Moreover, if A=In and ∑irank(Ai)=n, then (ii) and (iii) hold.

thm-mat-partitioned-inverse.title: Partitioned inverse
thm-mat-partitioned-inverse.html:
Let A be partitioned as in @eq-mat-partition with A11 nonsingular. Then A is nonsingular iff A22⋅1 is, and in that case A−1=(A11−1+A11−1A12A22⋅1−1A21A11−1−A11−1A12A22⋅1−1−A22⋅1−1A21A11−1A22⋅1−1).{#eq-mat-partitioned-inverse}

If A22 is also nonsingular, the leading block of A−1 equals A11⋅2−1: (A11−A12A22−1A21)−1=A11−1+A11−1A12A22⋅1−1A21A11−1.{#eq-mat-leading-block}

thm-mat-pd-characterizations.title: Characterizations
thm-mat-pd-characterizations.html:
For a symmetric n×n matrix A the following are equivalent:

  1. A is positive definite;

  2. every eigenvalue of A is positive;

  3. A=B⊤B for some matrix B with n columns and full column rank;

  4. A=LL⊤ with L lower triangular with positive diagonal entries (the Cholesky factorization; L is unique);

  5. every leading principal minor detA[k], k=1,…,n, is positive, where A[k] is the upper left k×k block.

Likewise, the following are equivalent: (a′) A is nonnegative definite; (b′) every eigenvalue is nonnegative; (c′) A=B⊤B for some B, which can be taken of size rank(A)×n; (e′) every principal minor (determinant of a submatrix with the same row and column indices) is nonnegative.

thm-mat-qr.title: Gram–Schmidt; QR factorization
thm-mat-qr.html: Let X=[x1,…,xp] be n×p with full column rank. Define recursively wj=xj−∑k<j(uk⊤xj)uk,uj=wj/‖wj‖. Then u1,…,up are orthonormal and, for each j, span the same subspace as x1,…,xj. Equivalently, X=QR with Q=[u1,…,up] satisfying Q⊤Q=Ip and R upper triangular with positive diagonal entries.

thm-mat-quadform-derivative.title: Derivatives of linear and quadratic forms
thm-mat-quadform-derivative.title_html: Derivatives of linear and quadratic forms
thm-mat-quadform-derivative.html: Let a∈Rn, let A be n×n and B be m×n. Then ∂(a⊤x)∂x=a,∂(Bx)∂x⊤=B,∂(x⊤Ax)∂x=(A+A⊤)x,∂2(x⊤Ax)∂x∂x⊤=A+A⊤. In particular ∂(x⊤Ax)/∂x=2Ax when A is symmetric.

thm-mat-rank-nullity.title: Rank–nullity
thm-mat-rank-nullity.html: For an m×n matrix A, rank(A)+dim⁡N(A)=n.

thm-mat-row-col-rank.title: Row rank equals column rank
thm-mat-row-col-rank.html: For every matrix A, dim⁡C(A⊤)=dim⁡C(A). That is, rank(A⊤)=rank(A). Moreover, if rank(A)=r≥1 there are an m×r matrix B and an r×n matrix F, both of rank r, with A=BF.

thm-mat-spectral.title: Spectral theorem
thm-mat-spectral.html:
Let A be an n×n symmetric matrix. Then all eigenvalues of A are real, and there is an orthogonal matrix Q=[q1,…,qn] with A=QΛQ⊤=∑i=1nλiqiqi⊤,Λ=diag(λ1,…,λn).{#eq-mat-spectral}

The columns of Q are an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, Aqi=λiqi. Eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.

thm-mat-square-root.title: Square root
thm-mat-square-root.html: A nonnegative definite matrix A=QΛQ⊤ has exactly one nonnegative definite matrix B with B2=A, namely A1/2=QΛ1/2Q⊤. It satisfies C(A1/2)=C(A). If A is positive definite, A1/2 is positive definite and its inverse is A−1/2=QΛ−1/2Q⊤.

thm-mat-svd.title: Singular value decomposition
thm-mat-svd.html:
Let A be m×n of rank r≥1. There are an m×r matrix U and an n×r matrix V, both with orthonormal columns, and numbers σ1≥⋯≥σr>0, such that A=UDV⊤=∑i=1rσiuivi⊤,D=diag(σ1,…,σr).{#eq-mat-svd}

The singular values σi are the positive square roots of the nonzero eigenvalues of A⊤A (equivalently of AA⊤). The columns of V and U are eigenvectors of A⊤A and AA⊤, with C(V)=C(A⊤) and C(U)=C(A). Moreover A+=VD−1U⊤ is the Moore–Penrose inverse of A.

thm-mat-trace-cyclic.title: Cyclic property
thm-mat-trace-cyclic.html: If A is m×n and B is n×m, then tr(AB)=tr(BA).

thm-mat-woodbury.title: Sherman–Morrison–Woodbury
thm-mat-woodbury.html:
Let B (n×n) and C (k×k) be nonsingular, and let U,V be n×k. If C−1+V⊤B−1U is nonsingular, then so is B+UCV⊤, and (B+UCV⊤)−1=B−1−B−1U(C−1+V⊤B−1U)−1V⊤B−1.{#eq-mat-woodbury}

In particular, for vectors u,v with 1+v⊤B−1u≠0, (B+uv⊤)−1=B−1−B−1uv⊤B−11+v⊤B−1u.{#eq-mat-sherman-morrison}
